concept.name: Upthrust
concept.definition: The Wyckoff event (UT) in which price moves above the resistance of a trading range and then quickly reverses to close back inside the range, acting as a test of remaining demand and a trap for uninformed breakout buyers. It is the mirror image of a spring.
concept.intuition: A fake breakout: price pops above resistance just long enough to hook breakout traders, then falls back into the range.
concept.mechanics: Price pushes above the resistance established by a buying climax or prior secondary tests, then reverses and closes below resistance. In Wyckoff analysis this shows large interests selling to breakout buyers; after an upthrust, price often tests the lower boundary of the range, and an upthrust occurring in Phase C of a distribution range is a candidate short area.
concept.failure_modes: Not every poke above resistance is an upthrust; if demand is genuine the breakout holds and becomes a jump to a higher range. Upthrusts also occur repeatedly in Phase B of ranges without any bearish resolution.
concept.misconceptions: An upthrust is not confirmed at its high; the bearish reading depends on the failure back into the range and subsequent weakness, and aggressive shorting at the first upthrust is repeatedly stopped out, as Wyckoff literature itself warns.
concept.example: A stock ranging between 136 and 150 spikes to 153 intraday but closes at 148; two weeks later it slides to the range bottom, completing the upthrust pattern.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
